title: A Comprehensive Review of Autophagy and Its Various Roles in Infectious, Non-Infectious, and Lifestyle Diseases: Current Knowledge and Prospects for Disease Prevention, Novel Drug Design, and Therapy

subsections.section_title: Molecular Mechanisms and Regulation of Autophagy: From Core Pathways to Signaling Networks
subsections.subsection_title: Core autophagy machinery and ATG protein functions
subsections.content:
Autophagy is orchestrated by a conserved set of autophagy-related (ATG) proteins that coordinate the formation and maturation of autophagosomes. The process initiates with the ULK1 complex (ULK1, ATG13, FIP200, ATG101), which integrates upstream signals to trigger phagophore nucleation. This is followed by the class III PI3K complex (VPS34, Beclin-1, ATG14, VPS15), which generates phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate to recruit downstream effectors to the phagophore assembly site. Two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems then mediate phagophore expansion: the ATG12–ATG5-ATG16L1 complex, which acts as an E3 ligase for LC3 lipidation, and the LC3/ATG8 family conjugation to phosphatidylethanolamine, enabling membrane curvature and cargo recruitment. ATG9, a transmembrane protein, shuttles membrane components from peripheral sites to the growing phagophore, while ATG2 facilitates lipid transfer from the ER. The ATG8 family proteins, including LC3B and GABARAPs, serve as scaffolds for selective autophagy receptors and are critical for autophagosome closure and cargo sequestration.

The precise spatiotemporal regulation of these ATG proteins ensures fidelity in autophagosome biogenesis. Mutations or dysregulation in ATG genes impair autophagic flux and are linked to neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, and infection susceptibility. Structural and biochemical studies have elucidated the molecular interfaces between ATG proteins, revealing how their interactions are dynamically modulated during autophagy progression.

subsections.section_title: Molecular Mechanisms and Regulation of Autophagy: From Core Pathways to Signaling Networks
subsections.subsection_title: Regulatory signaling pathways: mTOR, AMPK, and transcriptional control
subsections.content:
The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 (mTORC1) is a central inhibitor of autophagy under nutrient-rich conditions, phosphorylating and suppressing the ULK1 and ATG13 components of the initiation complex. Upon nutrient deprivation or energy stress, mTORC1 inactivation permits ULK1 activation, triggering phagophore formation ref [20]. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) acts as a key energy sensor that promotes autophagy through dual mechanisms: direct phosphorylation and activation of ULK1 at distinct sites, and inhibition of mTORC1 via TSC2 and Raptor phosphorylation ref [21]. AMPK also enhances autophagy by phosphorylating Beclin-1, promoting VPS34 complex assembly and PI3P generation ref [22]. Transcriptional regulation of autophagy is mediated by the TFEB/TFE3 family of bHLH-Zip transcription factors, which are inhibited by mTORC1-mediated cytoplasmic retention under fed conditions. Upon starvation or lysosomal stress, TFEB/TFE3 translocate to the nucleus and activate genes encoding autophagy and lysosomal components, including LC3, p62, and V-ATPase subunits ref [23]. The FOXO family of transcription factors, activated under low insulin/IGF-1 signaling, also induce autophagy-related gene expression, particularly in muscle and neuronal tissues ref [24]. Additionally, p53 can exert both pro- and anti-autophagic effects depending on its subcellular localization, with nuclear p53 promoting transcription of DRAM and Sestrin2, while cytoplasmic p53 inhibits autophagy ref [25].

The interplay between mTOR, AMPK, and transcriptional regulators forms a dynamic feedback network that fine-tunes autophagic flux in response to metabolic cues. Sestrin2, induced by p53 and AMPK, acts as a leucine sensor that inhibits mTORC1 by activating GATOR2 ref [26]. Conversely, mTORC1 suppresses TFEB activity by phosphorylating its serine residues, promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration ref [27]. Recent studies reveal that AMPK directly phosphorylates TFEB at Ser467, enhancing its nuclear translocation independently of mTORC1 ref [28]. Furthermore, the transcription factor NRF2, activated under oxidative stress, upregulates p62 and other autophagy genes, linking redox homeostasis to autophagic clearance ref [29]. Epigenetic regulators such as SIRT1 deacetylate and activate both FOXO3 and LC3, integrating metabolic signaling with chromatin-level control of autophagy ref [30]. The coordinated action of these pathways ensures that autophagy is precisely calibrated to cellular energy status, organelle integrity, and proteostatic demands.

subsections.section_title: Molecular Mechanisms and Regulation of Autophagy: From Core Pathways to Signaling Networks
subsections.subsection_title: Selective autophagy subtypes: mitophagy, xenophagy, lipophagy, and aggrephagy
subsections.content:
Selective autophagy subtypes target specific cargoes for degradation, ensuring cellular homeostasis under diverse stress conditions. Mitophagy, the selective removal of damaged mitochondria, is mediated by PINK1 and Parkin, which ubiquitinate outer mitochondrial membrane proteins to recruit autophagy adaptors such as OPTN and NDP52, leading to LC3 recruitment and engulfment [1]. Alternative mitophagy pathways involve receptors like BNIP3, NIX, and FUNDC1, which directly bind LC3 under hypoxic or stress conditions [2]. Xenophagy targets intracellular pathogens, with ubiquitin-coated bacteria recognized by p62/SQSTM1, NDP52, and OPTN, which bridge cargo to the autophagic machinery via LC3 interaction [3]. Lipophagy mediates the lysosomal degradation of lipid droplets through direct interaction of LC3 with lipid droplet-associated proteins such as PLIN2 and ATG14L, promoting fatty acid release during energy stress [4]. Aggrephagy clears toxic protein aggregates via p62/SQSTM1 and NBR1, which oligomerize and bind both ubiquitinated substrates and LC3, facilitating their sequestration into autophagosomes [5].

The specificity of these pathways is further fine-tuned by post-translational modifications and regulatory proteins. For instance, TBK1 phosphorylates autophagy receptors like OPTN and p62 to enhance their affinity for LC3 and ubiquitin [6]. In mitophagy, the deubiquitinase USP30 counteracts Parkin-mediated ubiquitination to limit excessive mitochondrial clearance [7]. Lipophagy is regulated by the transcription factor TFEB, which upregulates lysosomal hydrolases and lipid transporters [8], while aggrephagy is impaired in neurodegenerative diseases such as Huntington’s and Alzheimer’s due to mutations in autophagy receptors or ubiquitin ligases [9]. Crosstalk between selective autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system ensures coordinated clearance of misfolded proteins and damaged organelles [10].

subsections.section_title: Molecular Mechanisms and Regulation of Autophagy: From Core Pathways to Signaling Networks
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy-lysosome axis and lysosomal dynamics
subsections.content:
The autophagy-lysosome axis represents a tightly coordinated system in which autophagosomes mature and fuse with lysosomes to enable cargo degradation. Lysosomal dynamics—including biogenesis, acidification, motility, and membrane repair—are essential for maintaining autophagic flux. The transcription factor TFEB orchestrates lysosomal biogenesis by activating genes encoding lysosomal hydrolases and membrane proteins, a process inhibited by mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation and cytosolic sequestration ref [35]. Upon nutrient deprivation or lysosomal stress, TFEB translocates to the nucleus, enhancing lysosomal capacity and promoting autophagosome-lysosome fusion ref [46]. Lysosomal acidification, mediated by the V-ATPase complex, is critical for hydrolase activation; disruptions in V-ATPase assembly impair autophagic degradation and lead to autophagosome accumulation ref [58]. Lysosomal positioning along microtubules, regulated by RAB7 and the dynein-dynactin complex, facilitates encounters with autophagosomes, while lysosomal membrane permeabilization triggers compensatory lysosomal repair via ESCRT machinery ref [59]. Additionally, lysosomal calcium release through TRPML1 channels modulates fusion events and autophagic clearance ref [60].

Lysosomal dysfunction is increasingly linked to neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases. Mutations in lysosomal genes such as CTSB, LAMP2, and ATP13A2 impair autophagic degradation and contribute to protein aggregate accumulation ref [61]. The lysosomal enzyme cathepsin D processes autophagy substrates and regulates TFEB activity, forming a feedback loop that fine-tunes degradation capacity ref [62]. Recent studies reveal that lysosomal reformation from autolysosomes, mediated by the retromer complex and VPS35, replenishes functional lysosomes to sustain autophagy ref [63]. Furthermore, lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP1 and LAMP2 serve as sensors for nutrient status and influence mTORC1 reactivation upon amino acid repletion ref [64]. The interplay between autophagosome maturation and lysosomal homeostasis is thus central to cellular adaptation under stress.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases: Host Defense, Pathogen Evasion, and Therapeutic Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Xenophagy: Targeting intracellular pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi)
subsections.content:
Xenophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of intracellular pathogens, is a critical cell-autonomous defense mechanism against bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Ubiquitin-coated pathogens are recognized by autophagy receptors such as p62/SQSTM1, NDP52, and optineurin, which bridge cargo to LC3-positive autophagosomal membranes via their LIR domains. For instance, Salmonella enterica is targeted by NDP52 and optineurin upon ubiquitination by E3 ligases like LRSAM1 and HOIP, initiating autophagic clearance ref [38]. Similarly, Mycobacterium tuberculosis is sequestered by autophagy receptors in response to damage to its vacuolar membrane, although it often evades complete degradation. Viral pathogens such as herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) and poliovirus are targeted by autophagy through recognition of viral components or damaged membranes, with ATG5 and ATG16L1 playing essential roles in restriction ref [44]. Fungal pathogens like Candida albicans are also subjected to xenophagic clearance, particularly in macrophages, where Dectin-1 signaling enhances autophagic flux ref [43]. The TBK1 kinase amplifies xenophagy by phosphorylating autophagy receptors, enhancing their affinity for ubiquitin and LC3 ref [49]. Selective autophagy of pathogens is further regulated by innate immune sensors, including cGAS-STING, which can trigger autophagy in response to cytosolic DNA from intracellular microbes ref [43].

Emerging evidence highlights the role of ubiquitin-like conjugation systems and membrane dynamics in pathogen targeting. The ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 complex facilitates LC3 lipidation on pathogen-containing vesicles, while ATG9 vesicles supply membrane for phagophore expansion around intracellular microbes ref [43]. Additionally, the VPS34-PI3K complex, regulated by ATG14L, generates phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate to recruit downstream effectors to the forming autophagosome ref [43]. Recent studies demonstrate that autophagy receptors can recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns directly, bypassing ubiquitin in some contexts, underscoring the adaptability of xenophagy ref [44]. The integration of xenophagy with interferon responses and inflammasome activation further illustrates its centrality in antimicrobial immunity.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases: Host Defense, Pathogen Evasion, and Therapeutic Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Pathogen countermeasures: Viral and bacterial evasion of autophagy
subsections.content:
Many intracellular pathogens have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to evade or subvert autophagy, turning a host defense into a niche for replication. Bacteria such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion and secrete effectors like ESAT-6 that disrupt autophagic flux, while Listeria monocytogenes uses ActA to polymerize actin and escape autophagic recognition ref [65]. Shigella flexneri expresses IcsB to mask its surface protein VirG from the autophagy receptor NDP52, thereby avoiding xenophagic targeting ref [66]. Viruses also exploit autophagy evasion: herpesviruses encode BCL-2 homologs that bind Beclin-1 to suppress autophagosome formation ref [67], and hepatitis C virus (HCV) cleaves ATG5 via its NS3/4A protease to block autophagic degradation ref [68]. Influenza A virus NS1 protein interferes with RIG-I signaling, dampening autophagy induction ref [69]. Some pathogens hijack autophagic membranes for replication; poliovirus and coxsackievirus induce autophagosome-like vesicles to facilitate RNA replication without triggering degradation ref [70]. Fungi like Cryptococcus neoformans survive within autophagosomes by preventing acidification and lysosomal fusion ref [71].

Pathogens further modulate autophagy through interference with ubiquitin signaling and autophagy receptor function. Salmonella Typhimurium secretes deubiquitinases (e.g., SseL) to remove ubiquitin tags from bacterial surfaces, impairing recognition by p62 and NDP52 ref [72]. Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) downregulates SQSTM1/p62 expression to evade autophagic clearance ref [73]. Additionally, Staphylococcus aureus produces toxins that disrupt LC3 lipidation and autophagosome maturation ref [74]. Viral proteins such as HIV-1 Nef bind to Beclin-1 and inhibit VPS34 activity, suppressing autophagy initiation ref [75]. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) LMP1 activates mTORC1 to suppress autophagy while promoting survival ref [76]. These evasion strategies highlight the evolutionary arms race between host autophagy and microbial pathogens, revealing key vulnerabilities for therapeutic intervention.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases: Host Defense, Pathogen Evasion, and Therapeutic Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in innate and adaptive immune modulation
subsections.content:
Autophagy plays a critical role in modulating both innate and adaptive immune responses beyond its canonical function in pathogen clearance. It facilitates the delivery of viral nucleic acids to endosomal TLRs, enhancing type I interferon production, as demonstrated in dendritic cells infected with influenza virus ref [47]. Autophagy also supports antigen presentation by delivering intracellular pathogens or their components to MHC class II loading compartments, thereby activating CD4+ T cells ref [45]. In macrophages, autophagy regulates inflammasome activation by removing damaged mitochondria that release ROS and mtDNA, thus limiting IL-1β secretion ref [58]. Furthermore, selective autophagy of signaling adaptors like STING and MAVS fine-tunes innate immune signaling to prevent hyperinflammation ref [68]. Autophagy contributes to T cell homeostasis by degrading intracellular proteins and organelles, influencing T cell survival and memory formation ref [40]. In B cells, autophagy supports antibody secretion by maintaining endoplasmic reticulum integrity and ER stress resolution ref [74]. The autophagy receptor p62/SQSTM1 also acts as a signaling scaffold for NF-κB activation, linking autophagy to inflammatory gene expression ref [46].

Defects in autophagy genes, such as ATG5 or ATG16L1, are associated with impaired T cell responses and increased susceptibility to chronic infections ref [19]. Autophagy deficiency in dendritic cells reduces cross-presentation of viral antigens to CD8+ T cells, compromising cytotoxic immunity ref [45]. Conversely, pathogens exploit autophagy to dampen immune activation; for instance, HIV-1 Nef inhibits autophagy to suppress antigen presentation and evade T cell recognition ref [45]. Similarly, Epstein-Barr virus LMP1 suppresses autophagy to promote survival of infected B cells and limit immune detection ref [38]. These findings underscore autophagy as a central node integrating cellular homeostasis with immune regulation, offering novel targets for immunomodulatory therapies in infectious diseases.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Infectious Diseases: Host Defense, Pathogen Evasion, and Therapeutic Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic targeting of autophagy in infectious disease
subsections.content:
Therapeutic modulation of autophagy holds promise for treating infectious diseases by enhancing pathogen clearance or inhibiting pathogen exploitation of autophagic machinery. Pharmacological inducers such as rapamycin and its analogs (rapalogs) activate autophagy via mTORC1 inhibition, enhancing clearance of intracellular bacteria like Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Salmonella enterica [62]. Similarly, the AMPK activator metformin promotes autophagy and reduces viral loads in influenza and dengue virus infections by stimulating ULK1 and Beclin-1 activity [30]. Small molecules targeting the ATG protein machinery, such as the Beclin-1 mimetic Tat-beclin 1, have demonstrated efficacy in reducing viral replication of herpesviruses and HIV-1 by restoring autophagic flux [49]. Conversely, inhibitors of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, like chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine, have been explored to block pathogen survival in compartments that require lysosomal degradation, particularly in infections by Chlamydia trachomatis and Cryptococcus neoformans [40].

Emerging strategies include targeted activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which enhances lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic capacity; compounds like trehalose and curcumin induce TFEB nuclear translocation and improve clearance of intracellular pathogens [75]. Additionally, gene therapy approaches restoring defective autophagy genes, such as ATG16L1 in Crohn’s disease-associated susceptibility to bacterial infection, are under preclinical investigation. Selective autophagy enhancers, including compounds that stabilize autophagy receptors like p62 or NDP52, are being developed to boost xenophagy without global autophagy induction [14]. Recent studies also highlight the potential of microRNA-based therapeutics to fine-tune autophagy; for instance, inhibition of miR-30 family members restores Beclin-1 expression and enhances antimicrobial autophagy [60].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Chronic Diseases: Neurodegeneration, Cancer, and Cardiovascular Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Neurodegenerative diseases: Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Huntington’s
subsections.content:
Autophagy plays a critical yet context-dependent role in neurodegenerative diseases, serving as a key mechanism for clearing toxic protein aggregates in Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Huntington’s diseases. In Alzheimer’s, impaired autophagic flux contributes to the accumulation of amyloid-β plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau tangles, with lysosomal dysfunction exacerbating proteotoxicity ref [67]. Genetic variants in autophagy-related genes, such as BIN1 and PICALM, are associated with increased Alzheimer’s risk, highlighting the pathway’s protective role ref [45]. In Parkinson’s disease, mutations in PINK1 and Parkin disrupt mitophagy, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and dopaminergic neuron loss ref [23]. The autophagy receptor p62/SQSTM1 is essential for aggregating misfolded α-synuclein, and its dysfunction correlates with disease progression ref [23]. Huntington’s disease, caused by polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin, is characterized by defective aggrephagy, where mutant huntingtin impairs cargo recognition and autophagosome transport ref [45].

Therapeutic strategies targeting autophagy induction, such as rapamycin analogs and TFEB activators, have shown promise in preclinical models by enhancing clearance of pathogenic proteins ref [36]. However, excessive or dysregulated autophagy may contribute to neuronal death, underscoring the need for precise modulation. Recent studies indicate that restoring lysosomal acidification and autophagosome-lysosome fusion can rescue neurodegeneration in Huntington’s models ref [67]. Moreover, TFEB overexpression enhances clearance of mutant huntingtin and improves motor function in vivo ref [36]. The interplay between autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system further complicates therapeutic targeting, as compensatory mechanisms may mask efficacy ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Chronic Diseases: Neurodegeneration, Cancer, and Cardiovascular Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Cancer: Tumor suppression versus tumor promotion
subsections.content:
Autophagy plays a dual role in cancer, acting as a tumor suppressor in early stages and a tumor promoter in established tumors. In preneoplastic lesions, autophagy eliminates damaged organelles and protein aggregates, limiting genomic instability and oxidative stress. Loss-of-function mutations in autophagy genes such as BECN1 and ATG5 are associated with increased tumorigenesis in mouse models and human cancers, underscoring its protective function ref [84]. Beclin 1 haploinsufficiency promotes spontaneous tumors, and monoallelic deletions of BECN1 are frequent in human breast, ovarian, and prostate cancers ref [85]. Autophagy also facilitates tumor suppression by enabling oncogene-induced senescence and preventing necrosis-driven inflammation ref [86].

Conversely, in established tumors, autophagy supports cancer cell survival under metabolic stress, hypoxia, and chemotherapy. Tumor cells upregulate autophagy to recycle nutrients and maintain energy homeostasis, enabling resistance to therapy and metastasis ref [87]. Inhibition of autophagy in advanced cancers sensitizes tumors to radiation and cytotoxic agents in preclinical models ref [88]. The autophagy receptor p62/SQSTM1 accumulates in autophagy-deficient tumors, activating NRF2 and promoting proliferation ref [89]. Moreover, autophagy sustains mitochondrial function in cancer cells through mitophagy, allowing adaptation to metabolic demands ref [90]. The context-dependent role of autophagy is further modulated by oncogenic signaling pathways such as RAS and MYC, which can induce autophagy to support tumor growth ref [91].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Chronic Diseases: Neurodegeneration, Cancer, and Cardiovascular Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Cardiovascular diseases: Atherosclerosis, heart failure, and ischemia-reperfusion injury
subsections.content:
Autophagy plays a context-dependent role in cardiovascular diseases, acting as a protective mechanism in atherosclerosis by clearing lipid-laden macrophages and reducing plaque instability. Impaired autophagy in vascular cells promotes foam cell formation and necrotic core expansion, while its enhancement attenuates lesion progression in murine models. In heart failure, basal autophagy maintains cardiomyocyte homeostasis by removing damaged organelles and misfolded proteins; however, chronic or excessive activation contributes to contractile dysfunction and cell death. Autophagy deficiency in cardiomyocytes leads to accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and protein aggregates, accelerating cardiac remodeling.

During ischemia-reperfusion injury, autophagy is rapidly induced as a cytoprotective response to clear damaged mitochondria and limit oxidative stress. Pharmacological or genetic enhancement of autophagy reduces infarct size and improves functional recovery in preclinical models. Conversely, inhibition of autophagy exacerbates tissue damage, underscoring its essential role in stress adaptation. The balance between protective and detrimental autophagy is regulated by signaling pathways including AMPK, mTOR, and SIRT1, which modulate autophagic flux in response to metabolic and oxidative cues.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Chronic Diseases: Neurodegeneration, Cancer, and Cardiovascular Disorders
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in metabolic and mitochondrial disorders
subsections.content:
Autophagy plays a critical role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis by regulating lipid and glycogen turnover, mitochondrial quality, and cellular energy balance. In metabolic disorders such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, impaired autophagy contributes to ectopic lipid accumulation, insulin resistance, and pancreatic β-cell dysfunction. Lipophagy, the selective degradation of lipid droplets, is mediated by autophagy receptors like p62 and is essential for hepatic and adipose tissue lipid mobilization, with its disruption linked to steatosis and metabolic syndrome ref [91]. Mitochondrial dysfunction, a hallmark of metabolic diseases, is counteracted by mitophagy, which removes damaged organelles via receptors such as NIX and FUNDC1 ref [101], [85]. Defects in PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy are observed in insulin-resistant tissues, exacerbating oxidative stress and reducing ATP production. Genetic ablation of Atg7 in liver or muscle impairs glucose tolerance and promotes lipid accumulation, underscoring autophagy’s protective role ref [114]. Conversely, excessive autophagy in adipose tissue may contribute to lipodystrophy and systemic metabolic dysregulation.

Therapeutic modulation of autophagy has shown promise in preclinical models: AMPK activators like metformin enhance autophagic flux and improve insulin sensitivity, while mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin reduce hepatic steatosis ref [94], [100]. TFEB overexpression promotes lysosomal biogenesis and ameliorates lipid storage defects in models of Niemann-Pick type C disease ref [48], [110]. Mutations in lysosomal genes, including those encoding NPC1 and GBA, disrupt autophagic flux and are directly linked to lysosomal storage disorders with secondary metabolic dysfunction ref [31]. Emerging evidence also implicates autophagy in the pathogenesis of mitochondrial myopathies and Leigh syndrome, where defective mitophagy leads to accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and bioenergetic failure. Restoring autophagic clearance through pharmacological or genetic means represents a viable strategy for treating these complex disorders.

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle Factors and Autophagy: Diet, Exercise, Aging, and Environmental Stressors
subsections.subsection_title: Caloric restriction and intermittent fasting as autophagy inducers
subsections.content:
Caloric restriction (CR) and intermittent fasting (IF) are among the most robust non-pharmacological inducers of autophagy, consistently shown to enhance autophagic flux across multiple tissues. CR reduces nutrient availability, leading to inhibition of mTORC1 and activation of AMPK, which together promote ULK1-dependent autophagosome initiation ref [122]. IF regimens, including time-restricted feeding and alternate-day fasting, similarly trigger autophagy by cycling between fed and fasted states, thereby enhancing lysosomal degradation and cellular clearance ref [123]. In the liver, CR upregulates autophagy genes via FOXO3 and TFEB, facilitating the removal of damaged organelles and protein aggregates ref [124]. In the brain, both CR and IF stimulate neuronal autophagy, contributing to neuroprotection and reduced accumulation of misfolded proteins implicated in neurodegenerative diseases ref [125]. Skeletal muscle exhibits increased autophagic activity during fasting, preserving proteostasis and mitochondrial quality ref [126]. These effects are mediated in part by SIRT1-dependent deacetylation of autophagy-related proteins, including LC3 and FOXO3, which enhances autophagic efficiency ref [108].

Emerging evidence indicates that CR and IF enhance mitophagy and lipophagy, reducing lipid accumulation and improving metabolic flexibility ref [42]. In adipose tissue, fasting-induced autophagy promotes lipolysis and energy mobilization, while in the heart, it mitigates age-related dysfunction ref [127]. The transcriptional regulator PPARα is activated during fasting and directly induces autophagy genes in the liver, linking nutrient sensing to autophagic output ref [34]. Furthermore, CR enhances lysosomal biogenesis through TFEB nuclear translocation, amplifying autophagic capacity beyond initiation ref [46]. Human studies confirm that short-term fasting increases autophagic markers in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and skeletal muscle, validating translational relevance ref [128]. The protective effects of CR and IF are attenuated in autophagy-deficient models, underscoring autophagy as a central mediator of their benefits ref [129].

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle Factors and Autophagy: Diet, Exercise, Aging, and Environmental Stressors
subsections.subsection_title: Exercise-induced autophagy in muscle, brain, and metabolic tissues
subsections.content:
Exercise induces autophagy in skeletal muscle, brain, and metabolic tissues through conserved signaling pathways involving AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition. In skeletal muscle, acute endurance exercise triggers ULK1 phosphorylation and LC3 lipidation, enhancing autophagic flux to remove damaged organelles and maintain proteostasis ref [86]. This response is amplified by increased intracellular calcium and ROS, which activate CAMKK2-AMPK signaling ref [112]. In the brain, physical activity upregulates autophagy in hippocampal and cortical neurons, promoting clearance of misfolded proteins and supporting cognitive resilience ref [121]. Exercise-induced autophagy in the liver and adipose tissue facilitates lipophagy and mitochondrial turnover, improving insulin sensitivity and metabolic flexibility ref [114]. The transcription factor KLF15 is upregulated by exercise and directly activates autophagy-related genes in muscle, linking mechanical and metabolic stimuli to autophagic adaptation ref [112]. In adipose tissue, exercise enhances autophagic degradation of lipid droplets via ATG proteins, reducing ectopic lipid accumulation ref [114]. The neuroprotective effects of exercise are partially mediated by BDNF-dependent induction of autophagy, which mitigates synaptic protein aggregation ref [121]. These tissue-specific responses underscore autophagy as a central mechanism by which exercise confers systemic health benefits.

Chronic exercise training further enhances basal autophagic capacity and improves autophagic flux efficiency, particularly in aging individuals where autophagic decline is pronounced. In aged muscle, exercise restores impaired mitophagy by upregulating PINK1/Parkin and NIX pathways, improving mitochondrial quality ref [121]. In the brain, long-term physical activity increases TFEB nuclear translocation, promoting lysosomal biogenesis and autophagosome clearance ref [121]. Exercise also modulates autophagy in pancreatic β-cells and hepatocytes, contributing to glucose homeostasis and reduced hepatic steatosis ref [114]. These adaptations are blunted in autophagy-deficient models, confirming the causal role of autophagy in exercise-mediated metabolic and neuroprotective benefits ref [86].

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle Factors and Autophagy: Diet, Exercise, Aging, and Environmental Stressors
subsections.subsection_title: Aging and decline in autophagic capacity
subsections.content:
Aging is associated with a progressive decline in autophagic capacity, contributing to the accumulation of damaged organelles, misfolded proteins, and lipid aggregates that drive cellular dysfunction and age-related pathologies. This decline is observed across multiple tissues, including the brain, liver, and skeletal muscle, and is linked to reduced expression and activity of core autophagy genes such as ATG5, ATG7, and BECN1. Impaired lysosomal acidification and diminished lysosomal hydrolase activity further compromise autophagic flux in aged organisms, leading to the buildup of autophagic substrates and disrupted proteostasis. Studies in model organisms demonstrate that genetic disruption of autophagy accelerates aging phenotypes, while its enhancement extends lifespan, underscoring its protective role. In mammals, reduced TFEB nuclear translocation and diminished SIRT1 activity impair transcriptional activation of autophagy and lysosomal genes during aging. Additionally, chronic mTORC1 activation and diminished AMPK signaling in aged tissues suppress autophagy initiation. Mitophagy, in particular, is significantly impaired with age, resulting in dysfunctional mitochondrial accumulation and increased oxidative stress, as evidenced in aged neurons and cardiomyocytes. The decline in selective autophagy pathways, including aggrephagy and lipophagy, further exacerbates proteotoxic and metabolic stress in aging cells.

Emerging evidence indicates that age-related epigenetic silencing of autophagy-related promoters and altered post-translational modifications of autophagy proteins contribute to this functional decline. Moreover, systemic inflammation and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors inhibit autophagy in neighboring cells, creating a feed-forward loop of cellular deterioration. Restoring autophagic activity in aged models—through pharmacological agents like rapamycin or genetic interventions—has been shown to mitigate neurodegeneration, improve metabolic function, and extend healthspan, highlighting autophagy as a central target for anti-aging interventions.

subsections.section_title: Lifestyle Factors and Autophagy: Diet, Exercise, Aging, and Environmental Stressors
subsections.subsection_title: Environmental toxins, pollution, and circadian disruption
subsections.content:
Environmental toxins and air pollution, including particulate matter (PM2.5), heavy metals (e.g., cadmium, lead), and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, impair autophagic flux by inducing oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and disruption of autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Chronic exposure to PM2.5 suppresses autophagy in lung epithelial cells and macrophages, contributing to chronic inflammation and pulmonary disease ref [130]. Cadmium exposure inhibits TFEB nuclear translocation, reducing lysosomal biogenesis and impairing clearance of damaged organelles ref [131]. Similarly, lead disrupts autophagic degradation by altering lysosomal pH and inhibiting cathepsin activity ref [132]. These disruptions promote proteotoxic stress and cellular senescence, accelerating age-related pathologies.

Circadian disruption, caused by shift work, jet lag, or light at night, dysregulates core clock genes (BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY) that directly control autophagy gene expression. BMAL1 transcriptionally regulates key autophagy components, including LC3 and ATG7, and its loss reduces basal autophagy in liver and muscle ref [37]. Disrupted circadian rhythms impair mitophagy and lipophagy, leading to metabolic dysfunction and lipid accumulation ref [133]. Moreover, circadian misalignment suppresses SIRT1 activity, diminishing its deacetylation of autophagy regulators such as LC3 and FOXO3 ref [30]. This circadian-autophagy axis is further compromised by environmental pollutants that alter melatonin signaling, a key modulator of autophagic timing ref [134].

Emerging evidence links chronic circadian disruption and toxin exposure to neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases through convergent suppression of autophagy. For instance, chronic exposure to diesel exhaust particles and circadian misalignment synergistically impair hippocampal autophagy, accelerating amyloid-β accumulation ref [135]. In adipose tissue, shift work-induced circadian disruption reduces autophagic clearance of lipid droplets, promoting insulin resistance ref [136]. These findings underscore the need for chronotherapeutic strategies to restore autophagic homeostasis in polluted and shift-work environments.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy as a Therapeutic Target: Pharmacological Modulators, Drug Design, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy inducers: Rapalogs, metformin, spermidine, and novel small molecules
subsections.content:
Rapalogs, such as rapamycin and its analogs (e.g., everolimus, temsirolimus), are well-established autophagy inducers that inhibit mTORC1, thereby relieving its suppression of the ULK1 complex and promoting autophagosome formation ref [17]. These agents have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of neurodegeneration, cancer, and aging by enhancing clearance of toxic protein aggregates and damaged organelles ref [17]. Metformin, a first-line antidiabetic drug, activates AMPK independently of LKB1, leading to mTORC1 inhibition and TFEB nuclear translocation, thereby stimulating autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis ref [20]. Clinical studies in type 2 diabetes and cancer patients suggest metformin’s autophagy-inducing effects contribute to its protective benefits ref [20]. Spermidine, a natural polyamine, induces autophagy by inhibiting EP300-mediated acetylation of autophagy-related proteins, including LC3 and ATG proteins, and has been shown to extend lifespan in model organisms ref [107]. Novel small molecules such as SMER28, Trehalose, and LYN-1604 have emerged as mTOR-independent autophagy inducers; SMER28 enhances autophagosome formation via unknown targets, while trehalose acts as a chemical chaperone that promotes TFEB activation ref [107]. LYN-1604 directly binds and activates Beclin 1, bypassing mTOR to initiate autophagy ref [104].

Recent efforts have focused on developing selective autophagy inducers targeting specific pathways, such as compounds that activate TFEB or enhance mitophagy. For instance, the small molecule 1,10-phenanthroline derivatives promote TFEB nuclear translocation and lysosomal gene expression, offering potential in lysosomal storage disorders ref [73]. Similarly, Urolithin A, a gut microbiome-derived metabolite, induces mitophagy and improves muscle function in aged mice by activating PINK1/Parkin signaling ref [118]. These agents represent a shift toward precision modulation, avoiding broad autophagy activation that may be detrimental in certain contexts. However, challenges remain in achieving tissue-specific delivery and avoiding off-target effects, particularly given the dual roles of autophagy in tumor suppression and cancer cell survival ref [135]. Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating the safety and efficacy of these inducers in neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s, with biomarker-guided dosing strategies under development ref [117].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy as a Therapeutic Target: Pharmacological Modulators, Drug Design, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy inhibitors: Chloroquine derivatives, lysosomal blockers, and combination therapies
subsections.content:
Chloroquine (CQ) and its derivative hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) are among the most widely studied autophagy inhibitors, acting by raising lysosomal pH and impairing autophagosome-lysosome fusion and cargo degradation. These agents have been evaluated in numerous clinical trials for cancer, often in combination with chemotherapy or targeted therapies, based on the premise that autophagy inhibition sensitizes tumor cells to stress-induced death. However, their lack of specificity and dose-limiting toxicities, including retinopathy and cardiomyopathy, have limited their therapeutic utility. More selective lysosomal inhibitors, such as bafilomycin A1 and concanamycin A, target the V-ATPase proton pump to block lysosomal acidification, thereby halting autophagic flux, as demonstrated in preclinical models of neurodegeneration and cancer ref [85]. Newer agents like Lys05, a dimeric CQ derivative with enhanced lysosomotropism, show improved potency in preclinical models of pancreatic and breast cancer ref [121].

Combination therapies exploiting autophagy inhibition have gained traction in oncology, particularly in contexts where tumors rely on autophagy for survival under metabolic or therapeutic stress. For instance, HCQ combined with gemcitabine or radiation has shown promise in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, while in melanoma, autophagy inhibition reverses resistance to BRAF and MEK inhibitors ref [102]. In glioblastoma, dual targeting of mTOR and autophagy with HCQ and temozolomide has yielded synergistic effects in preclinical models ref [100]. Emerging strategies include co-targeting lysosomal function with proteasome inhibitors, exploiting proteotoxic stress in multiple myeloma ref [121]. Recent efforts focus on developing lysosome-specific inhibitors with improved pharmacokinetics, such as the cathepsin inhibitor E64d and the TRPML1 antagonist ML-SI1, which disrupt autolysosomal maturation without systemic toxicity ref [86].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy as a Therapeutic Target: Pharmacological Modulators, Drug Design, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Targeting selective autophagy pathways for precision therapy
subsections.content:
Selective autophagy pathways—such as mitophagy, aggrephagy, xenophagy, and lipophagy—offer precise therapeutic opportunities by targeting specific cargo for degradation, minimizing off-target effects. In neurodegenerative diseases, enhancing aggrephagy via modulation of p62/SQSTM1 or OPTN/NDP52 receptors can clear toxic protein aggregates, as demonstrated in models of Alzheimer’s and Huntington’s disease ref [41]. Mitophagy restoration through activation of PINK1/Parkin or FUNDC1 pathways has shown efficacy in Parkinson’s and heart failure models ref [92], ref [54]. In infection, targeting xenophagy by stabilizing ubiquitin coatings on pathogens or inhibiting bacterial deubiquitinases like SseL can enhance pathogen clearance ref [86], ref [88]. Cancer cells exploit selective autophagy to survive metabolic stress; inhibiting lipophagy via ATG14L suppression or activating mitophagy to eliminate dysfunctional mitochondria in RAS-driven tumors represents emerging strategies ref [8], ref [80]. TBK1-mediated phosphorylation of autophagy receptors enhances cargo recognition, making it a druggable node for precision modulation ref [95].

Emerging small molecules, such as urolithin A (inducing mitophagy) and carnosine (promoting aggrephagy), are in preclinical development, while CRISPR-based screening has identified novel selective autophagy regulators like ZKSCAN3 and MCOLN1 ref [104], ref [105]. Precision targeting requires biomarkers of cargo-specific flux, such as mitochondrial DNA turnover for mitophagy or lipid droplet loss for lipophagy. Combining selective autophagy modulators with conventional therapies—e.g., enhancing xenophagy alongside antibiotics in persistent infections—holds promise for synergistic efficacy without systemic autophagy disruption.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy as a Therapeutic Target: Pharmacological Modulators, Drug Design, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Biomarkers of autophagic flux and clinical monitoring
subsections.content:
Accurate assessment of autophagic flux is essential for evaluating therapeutic efficacy and disease progression in clinical settings. The most widely used biomarkers include LC3-II turnover, p62/SQSTM1 degradation, and lysosomal protease activity, which collectively reflect autophagosome formation, cargo delivery, and degradation. Immunoblotting of LC3-II in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors remains a gold standard for measuring flux in tissues and cell lines, while immunohistochemical detection of LC3 puncta provides spatial resolution in biopsy samples. However, these methods are often limited by tissue heterogeneity and technical variability, prompting the development of more robust in vivo reporters such as GFP-LC3-RFP-LC3ΔG (mRFP-GFP-LC3) transgenic models, which distinguish autophagosomes (yellow) from autolysosomes (red) based on pH-dependent fluorescence quenching [1].

Emerging non-invasive biomarkers include circulating autophagy-related proteins and microRNAs, such as serum p62, LC3B, and miR-30a, which correlate with autophagic activity in neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases [2,3]. In cancer, elevated plasma p62 levels predict poor response to mTOR inhibitors, while reduced autophagosome-associated vesicles in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) indicate impaired flux in aging and Alzheimer’s disease [4,5]. Advanced imaging techniques, including PET tracers targeting lysosomal cathepsins or autophagy receptors, are under clinical validation for real-time monitoring [6]. Additionally, mass spectrometry-based proteomics has identified novel flux-sensitive peptides derived from autophagy substrates, offering high specificity for patient stratification [7].

Standardization of sampling protocols, timing, and analytical platforms remains a major challenge. The Autophagy Guideline Consortium has proposed consensus criteria for biomarker validation, emphasizing paired measurements with and without lysosomal inhibition and the use of multiple complementary readouts [8]. Integration of these biomarkers into clinical trials for autophagy-modulating therapies—such as hydroxychloroquine in cancer or rapalogs in neurodegeneration—is critical for dose optimization and patient selection [9,10].

subsections.section_title: Integrative Perspectives: Systems Biology, Personalized Medicine, and Future Directions in Autophagy Research
subsections.subsection_title: Systems biology approaches to map autophagy networks in disease
subsections.content:
Systems biology approaches have enabled the comprehensive mapping of autophagy networks across disease contexts by integrating multi-omics data, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, to reconstruct dynamic regulatory circuits. High-throughput screening and network modeling have identified context-specific autophagy modules in cancer, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders, revealing non-canonical interactions beyond core ATG proteins. For instance, integrative analyses of patient-derived tissues have uncovered disease-associated autophagy signatures linked to TFEB target genes and lysosomal enzyme expression patterns, providing mechanistic insights into autophagic failure in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases. Network inference algorithms have further revealed crosstalk between autophagy and immune signaling pathways, such as NF-κB and STING, in tumor microenvironments. Computational models incorporating protein-protein interaction data and flux measurements have predicted key regulatory nodes, including ULK1 and VPS34, as critical hubs whose perturbation alters autophagic output in a tissue-dependent manner. These approaches have also identified novel autophagy regulators through guilt-by-association analyses in large-scale datasets, such as the role of KLF15 in muscle-specific autophagy and the involvement of TRPML1 in lysosomal calcium-mediated autophagosome maturation.

Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing have resolved heterogeneity in autophagy gene expression across cell types within diseased tissues, demonstrating that autophagic activity varies significantly between neurons, microglia, and astrocytes in neurodegenerative brains. Multi-omics integration has further linked epigenetic modifications, such as histone acetylation at ATG promoters, to altered autophagy in aging and metabolic syndrome. Systems-level analyses of autophagy substrates have revealed disease-specific cargo profiles, including aggregated proteins in neurodegeneration and damaged mitochondria in cardiomyopathies. These findings underscore the necessity of context-aware models for therapeutic targeting, moving beyond blanket autophagy induction or inhibition. The convergence of network pharmacology and flux-based modeling now enables predictive simulation of autophagy modulation under genetic or pharmacological perturbations, guiding precision intervention strategies.

subsections.section_title: Integrative Perspectives: Systems Biology, Personalized Medicine, and Future Directions in Autophagy Research
subsections.subsection_title: Personalized autophagy modulation: Genetic, epigenetic, and microbiome influences
subsections.content:
Genetic variation significantly influences autophagy efficiency and disease susceptibility, with polymorphisms in ATG5, ATG16L1, and IRGM linked to altered autophagic responses in Crohn’s disease and tuberculosis [1]. Rare loss-of-function mutations in BECN1 and SQSTM1 predispose individuals to neurodegenerative and oncogenic conditions, underscoring the need for genotype-stratified therapeutic approaches [2]. Epigenetic regulation further fine-tunes autophagy through DNA methylation of LC3 and BECN1 promoters in aging and metabolic syndrome, while histone modifications by HDACs and HATs modulate TFEB and FOXO3 transcriptional activity in response to nutrient cues [3]. MicroRNA-30 family members suppress autophagy by targeting BECN1 and ATG5, and their expression varies across tissues and individuals, offering biomarkers for personalized modulation [4].

The gut microbiome exerts systemic influence on autophagy via microbial metabolites such as butyrate, which activates SIRT1 and AMPK to enhance autophagic flux, and lipopolysaccharide, which inhibits TFEB nuclear translocation [5]. Germ-free mice exhibit impaired autophagy in intestinal epithelia, reversed by fecal transplantation, highlighting microbiota-dependent regulation [6]. Specific bacterial strains, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, induce autophagy via TLR2 signaling, while pathobionts like Enteropathogenic E. coli disrupt autophagosome maturation through effector proteins [7]. Interindividual microbiome diversity thus contributes to variable responses to dietary interventions and pharmacological autophagy inducers [8].

Integrating genetic, epigenetic, and microbiome data enables predictive modeling of autophagy phenotypes, facilitating precision interventions. For instance, carriers of ATG16L1 T300A may benefit from butyrate supplementation, while individuals with hypermethylated BECN1 promoters may respond to HDAC inhibitors [9]. Emerging multi-omics frameworks are beginning to map these interactions, revealing how host genotype shapes microbial colonization, which in turn modulates epigenetic marks on autophagy genes [10].

subsections.section_title: Integrative Perspectives: Systems Biology, Personalized Medicine, and Future Directions in Autophagy Research
subsections.subsection_title: Challenges in clinical translation: Heterogeneity, timing, and tissue specificity
subsections.content:
Clinical translation of autophagy-modulating therapies is hindered by profound interindividual heterogeneity in autophagic responses, driven by genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors. Genome-wide association studies have identified polymorphisms in autophagy-related genes, such as ATG16L1, that alter flux and disease susceptibility in a tissue-specific manner, complicating universal therapeutic design ref [121]. Moreover, autophagic activity varies dramatically across tissues—e.g., hepatic autophagy is highly responsive to fasting, while neuronal autophagy is more constitutively active yet vulnerable to age-related decline ref [151]. This tissue specificity is further complicated by cell-type heterogeneity within organs, as single-cell RNA sequencing reveals distinct autophagy signatures in microglia versus neurons in Parkinson’s disease ref [176].

Timing of intervention presents another critical challenge: autophagy can be protective or detrimental depending on disease stage. In early cancer, autophagy suppresses tumorigenesis, but in advanced stages, it supports tumor survival under metabolic stress ref [127]. Similarly, in neurodegeneration, early autophagy induction may clear toxic aggregates, whereas chronic activation may exhaust cellular resources ref [182]. The dynamic nature of autophagic flux, influenced by circadian rhythms and metabolic cycles, further demands precise temporal targeting ref [138].

Current biomarkers lack the sensitivity to capture these nuances in real time across tissues. While plasma LC3B-II and serum p62 are used as surrogates, their correlation with tissue-specific flux remains inconsistent ref [173], [175]. Standardization of biopsy-based autophagy assessment is urgently needed to account for sampling variability and methodological differences ref [177]. Without resolving these challenges, personalized autophagy modulation will remain empiric rather than mechanistic.

subsections.section_title: Integrative Perspectives: Systems Biology, Personalized Medicine, and Future Directions in Autophagy Research
subsections.subsection_title: Future directions: Gene therapy, nanotechnology, and AI-driven drug discovery
subsections.content:
Gene therapy holds promise for restoring autophagic function in monogenic disorders by targeting core ATG genes or transcription factors such as TFEB. Recent studies demonstrate that AAV-mediated TFEB overexpression enhances clearance of toxic protein aggregates in models of Huntington’s disease and improves cardiac function in pressure overload, suggesting therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative and cardiovascular conditions [1]. Similarly, CRISPR-Cas9 correction of ATG16L1 polymorphisms in intestinal organoids rescues autophagic flux and reduces inflammatory responses, offering a precision medicine approach for Crohn’s disease [2].

Nanotechnology enables tissue-specific delivery of autophagy modulators, overcoming systemic toxicity and bioavailability limitations. Lipid nanoparticles loaded with siRNA against mTOR or chloroquine analogs have shown enhanced autophagic induction in brain and tumor tissues, with improved biodistribution and reduced off-target effects [3]. Additionally, exosome-based delivery of autophagy-inducing miRNAs, such as miR-30a inhibitors, has been shown to restore mitophagy in cardiomyocytes and reduce ischemic injury [4]. Engineered nanocarriers functionalized with lysosome-targeting peptides facilitate precise lysosomal delivery of activators, enhancing autophagosome-lysosome fusion in aged or diseased tissues [5].

AI-driven drug discovery is accelerating the identification of novel autophagy modulators by integrating multi-omics data, protein interaction networks, and deep learning. Machine learning models trained on autophagy-related transcriptomes and proteomes have predicted novel small-molecule inducers of TFEB nuclear translocation, validated in high-throughput screens [6]. Graph neural networks have identified synergistic drug combinations targeting ULK1 and VPS34 in KRAS-mutant cancers, improving efficacy over monotherapy [7]. Furthermore, generative AI has designed novel autophagy-enhancing peptides with high binding affinity to p62, validated by structural modeling and cellular assays [8]. These approaches, combined with digital twins of autophagy networks, are poised to transform personalized therapeutic design [9].
